summary: Discovery focused on embeddings + reranking integration and whether Quasar should use Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, or Private. Main concerns: vector DB integration, throughput/latency for 200-500k docs, embedding dimensionality (128 vs 768), hybrid search with lexical + vector, security (SOC2, KMS), and cost trade-offs for dedicated capacity. Agreed next steps: Redwood to send pricing, security docs, and run a bench POC with sample data.
topics: Intro & context; Current search architecture; Embeddings strategy; Vector DB and hybrid search; Throughput and latency targets; Deployment modes (hosted/dedicated/private); Security/compliance; POC scope & next steps
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, this is Priya our SE. how's everyone's afternoon?
[00:06] Maya Patel: Good, thanks. really looking forward to this, we want to replace a lot of our TF-IDF bumping with embeddings + rerank.
[00:12] Alex Kim: Awesome. Can you start with a quick overview of Quasar's current infra and the problem you're solving?
[00:18] Maya Patel: Sure, so right now we run Elastic in a managed cluster, about 10 nodes, we do lexical search, some rule-based boosting. we ingest ~350k docs, roughly 50M tokens, and search traffic is spiky - peak qps around 120 reads/sec. our latency p90 needs to stay under 120ms for SERP responses.
[00:33] Carlos Jimenez: Adding embeddings we want semantic recall for long-tail queries but still keep lexical signals. so hybrid search is a must.
[00:40] Priya Shah: That makes sense. are you planning to store vectors in Elastic, or use a vector store like Pinecone/PQ or self-managed FAISS?
[00:48] Liam O'Connor: We're evaluating. We currently push some embeddings to a prototype Pinecone set, but cost and vendor lock are concerns. also, we have strict data residency for EU users.
[00:58] Alex Kim: Got it. From Redwood side, we support three modes - hosted API, dedicated pools, and private VPC/on-prem. For vector DB integration, we typically do two patterns: 1) Redwood generates embeddings and you index them in your vector DB and call Redwood for generation/rerank, or 2) Redwood can host embeddings + reranking path and return re-ranked ids so you don't need a separate service.
[01:20] Maya Patel: Option 2 sounds interesting - fewer moving parts. But what's the throughput? our peaks need to handle batching and also low-latency single queries.
[01:28] Priya Shah: Right - for reranking we usually do a two-stage flow: candidate retrieval from your vector DB (ANN) and then a lightweight reranker that scores top-N candidates. In hosted mode we can do the rerank in ~40-80ms for a 128-dim embedding and top-10 candidates on a small model; with dedicated capacity you can push that under 30ms consistently since you get pinned GPUs and predictable batching.
[01:45] Carlos Jimenez: Wait, you said 128-dim - we're using 768-dim embeddings from our prototype model. will that affect latency?
[01:53] Priya Shah: Yes - dimensionality impacts compute and memory. 768 dims will increase the rerank compute, roughly proportional. we often recommend 128 or 256 for production retrieval + a stronger reranker model. But if you need semantic fidelity from 768, we can support it; dedicated or private tends to be the better fit for higher-dim production at scale.
[02:10] Liam O'Connor: How about hybrid search - we need hybrid scoring that blends BM25 with vector similarity. do you have examples customers use?
[02:16] Alex Kim: Absolutely. Typical pattern: run lexical recall in Elastic, run vector ANN for semantic candidates, union results, and then rerank with Redwood which can incorporate lexical signals passed as features. we also support an in-line hybrid scoring where we pass token-level or BM25 proxy scores into the reranker.
[02:33] Maya Patel: One of our concerns is vector DB vendor lock and moving vectors between environments. how easy is it to migrate?
[02:39] Priya Shah: Pretty straightforward. We export embeddings as standard float arrays and we support common index formats (faiss, hnsw). For moving between hosted/dedicated/private you can keep the same embeddings; the reranker is stateless. the KV cache comment: also some mis-transcriptions earlier said K-V cash but it's K V cache - we manage remote KV cache for generation models but for rerank it's ephemeral.
[02:59] Carlos Jimenez: Security - we need SOC2, SSO, audit logs, and KMS integration. if we do private deployment we need customer-managed KMS.
[03:07] Alex Kim: Redwood supports SOC2 and can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for private deployments. Hosted has BYOK options too in many regions. we also provide audit logs and role-based access. we'll share the security whitepaper after the call.
[03:18] Maya Patel: Cost - can you ballpark hosted vs dedicated for our traffic?
[03:22] Alex Kim: Ballpark: hosted per request/embedding units will generally be lower OpEx for low to medium volume. For sustained high qps and strict p90 SLAs, dedicated reserved capacity often reduces unit cost by 30-50% at commit levels. exact math depends on batching, sequence lengths, and embedding dim. we'll send a modeled estimate.
[03:40] Priya Shah: Also batching and prefix/KV caching help reduce per-token cost for generation-heavy rerankers. for pure rerank, the top-K scoring pattern is the main cost driver.
[03:48] Liam O'Connor: Throughput - what's the expected indexing throughput if we want to re-embed 350k docs? we need a window of a couple days.
[03:55] Priya Shah: For bulk embedding jobs, hosted parallel ingestion can handle many thousands per minute depending on tokenization. dedicated jobs with multi-GPU parallelism will finish fastest; we can also provide out-of-band bulk ingest pipelines. we'll include recommended chunking and rate limits in the benchmark doc.
[04:10] Carlos Jimenez: Latency SLOs - you mentioned 30ms under dedicated. what's realistic for hybrid search end-to-end including Elastic candidate retrieval?
[04:16] Alex Kim: If Elastic retrieval is local and fast (say 15-30ms), and your ANN returns top-100 in ~20ms, and Redwood rerank is ~30-60ms, end-to-end 120-180ms is reasonable. you can optimize candidate set size and model size to hit your 120ms p90 target. that's why we recommend doing an initial POC with your dataset and traffic pattern.
[04:37] Maya Patel: POC scope - can we do 200k docs and simulate traffic spikes to 150 qps?
[04:42] Priya Shah: Yes, that scope is doable. we'll define ingestion steps, sample queries, and metrics: p50/p90 latency, recall@10, MRR, and cost per query.
[04:52] Alex Kim: Quick qual question - who's going to own the POC internally?
[04:55] Maya Patel: Carlos will own the engineering work, I'll own product acceptance. Liam will sign off on procurement.
[05:02] Liam O'Connor: For procurement - we need standard terms + data residency annex.
[05:06] Alex Kim: Noted. we'll surface regional availability and contract templates.
[05:10] Carlos Jimenez: A couple of nitty-gritty items: does Redwood support HNSW parameters tuning (M, ef_construction) via API or do we need to manage that ourselves?
[05:17] Priya Shah: We don't manage your ANN index tuning if you're self-hosting. if you use Redwood-hosted vector index options we expose tuning knobs or recommend config defaults depending on latency/recall tradeoffs.
[05:27] Maya Patel: Any known gotchas when switching from 768->256 dims? we saw recall drop for certain query types.
[05:32] Priya Shah: There's often a tradeoff - lower dims reduce ANN memory and latency but can hurt fine-grained distinctions. a common approach: use 256 for retrieval and keep a higher-dim embedding for offline tasks or re-embedding specific heavy-duty queries. also consider using quantization for storage savings if you're cost-sensitive.
[05:50] Alex Kim: Ok, let's recap next steps: we'll send pricing and security docs, Priya will prepare POC plan and ingestion checklist, Quasar to share sample dataset and define acceptance metrics, and we schedule a SE deep dive next week.
[06:02] Maya Patel: Sounds good. thanks everyone.
[06:05] Alex Kim: Thanks, talk soon.
[06:07] [meeting ends]
